sections.title: Build your introduction from four lines
body: Copy whole chunks before studying grammar: Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar …
Jag bor i tells where you live now. Jag kommer från tells where you come from. The places can be different.
Use och before the last language. Put lite directly before a language you speak only a little.

activity.pattern: Many language names end in -ska: finska, svenska, ryska, tyska, turkiska, kinesiska, engelska. Countries take a capital letter; languages do not. Hindi and urdu keep their own names, and the language is hindi, not hindu.

sections.title: Nine vowels: copy the mouth first
body: Swedish has nine vowel letters: A, O, U, Y, I, E, Ö, Ä, Å. First copy the lip and tongue position; then copy the audio.
English, Hindi, and Marathi examples are memory bridges, not exact Swedish pronunciation. The Swedish recording is the final model.
Rounded lips: O, U, Y, Ö, Å. Front tongue: I, E, Y, Ä, Ö. Notice that Y and Ö belong to both groups.

examples.note: Open for A; round for O.
Keep the lips rounded; move the tongue forward for Y.

examples.en: I, E, Ö, Ä, and Å lesson words
examples.note: Compare the mouth shapes; do not force an English sound.

rows: Deep and open; आ is a starting bridge
Round lips; often near long oo in these words
Tight rounded lips; no exact English/Hindi match
Keep the I/ई tongue, then round the lips
Wide smile; ई is a starting bridge
Light smile; ए is a starting bridge
Keep the E tongue, then round the lips
Relaxed open front sound; near e in bed
Deep rounded sound; ऑ/aw is a starting bridge

sections.memoryTip: The script cue helps you find the mouth. It does not replace listening: Swedish audio wins.
sections.tryIt: Use a mirror: say I → Y without moving the tongue, only rounding the lips. Then say E → Ö the same way.

activity.label: Mouth map
activity.title: Explore the nine vowels one mouth at a time
activity.instructions: Tap a vowel, copy the mouth cue, and hear its lesson words. Then light up a group to see which vowels share a mouth shape.

features.label: Rounded lips
features.note: O, U, Y, Ö and Å push the lips forward into a circle. Check in a mirror.

features.label: Front vowels
features.note: E, I, Y, Ä and Ö keep the tongue forward. Remember this group: it softens g, k and sk in topic 4.

sounds.cue: Open wide and let the sound sit at the back of the mouth. आ is a starting bridge.
Round the lips as in boots. In these words Swedish O sounds close to a long oo.
Tight rounded lips, as if drinking through a straw. Long u in du and short u in dum sound different: copy each one.
Say I, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for U.
Wide smile, tongue high and forward. ई is a starting bridge.
A lighter smile than I. ए is a starting bridge.
Say E, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for O.
Drop the jaw as for A, but aim for E. Near the e in bed.
The real O: deep and round. ऑ or English aw is a starting bridge.

contrasts.label: I → Y
contrasts.audio: i, y. i, y. Kina, by.
contrasts.cue: Tongue stays still. Only the lips round.

contrasts.label: E → Ö
contrasts.audio: e, ö. e, ö. le, ö.
contrasts.cue: Same trick: keep the E tongue, round the lips.

contrasts.label: O → Å
contrasts.cue: Swedish O often sounds like oo. The O you know from English is usually written Å.

sections.title: Long or short: stretch one part
body: In a stressed Swedish syllable, either the vowel is long or the consonant after it is long. Hear both parts, not only the vowel.

A common spelling clue is: one consonant letter after the stressed vowel often means a longer vowel; a doubled consonant often means a short vowel and longer consonant. It is a clue, not a rule without exceptions.
Use the routine: find the stressed vowel → look right → listen → copy the whole word.

examples.note: Stretch the a in tak; stop it quickly and hold the k in tack.
Hear the stressed final é in kafé and the short a plus long f in kaffe.
Bor has a long stressed vowel; the doubled consonants signal short stressed vowels in the other words.

rows: cut the vowel; hold the consonant

sections.memoryTip: Single often means STRETCH. Double often means STOP the vowel quickly—but always check the stressed syllable and listen.
sections.tryIt: Say tak—tack three times. Make the contrast bigger than feels natural, then say the pair normally.

activity.label: Stretch or stop?
activity.title: Predict the length from the spelling, then check by ear
activity.instructions: Look at the highlighted stressed vowel and the letters after it. Choose stretch or stop, then play the word to confirm.

buckets.label: Stretch
buckets.hint: long vowel · one consonant after it

buckets.label: Stop
buckets.hint: short vowel · two consonants after it

items.why: One k after the a: stretch the a.
ck counts as a double consonant: cut the a and hold the k.
One k after the o: stretch it.
Double f: a short a and a long f.
One r after the o: stretch it.
Double m: stop the a quickly and hold the m.
Nothing follows the stressed y, so it is long.
Double p: short a, long p.
One n after the å: stretch it.
Double t: short ö, long t.
Two different consonants, s and t, also usually mean a short vowel.
Double g after the stressed u: keep the u short.

activity.summary: One consonant after the stressed vowel usually means stretch. Two consonants usually mean stop. It is a strong clue, not a law, so the recording always has the final say.

sections.title: One vowel group, three soft sounds
body: The spelling group E, I, Y, Ä, Ö often softens the consonant immediately before it. These are front vowels because the tongue is forward; Y and Ö still use rounded lips.
G usually becomes the Swedish j sound, K usually becomes the tj sound /ɕ/, and SK usually becomes the sj sound /ɧ/ before this group.
TJ is not exactly English ch, and SJ is not exactly English sh. Use the shortcut to predict, then use audio to learn the actual sound. Some loanwords are exceptions.

examples.note: The first vowel is Ä or I.
Make a narrow, light sound; do not add an English t + ch.
This sound varies by region and speaker.

examples.en: hard sk before A and U
examples.note: No front vowel follows sk.
One short sentence for repeated K + front-vowel practice.

rows: g + e, i, y, ä, ö
k + e, i, y, ä, ö
sk + e, i, y, ä, ö

sections.memoryTip: Same five vowels, three different results: G → J, K → TJ, SK → SJ. Do not call all three ‘sh’.
sections.tryIt: Underline the first vowel in gillar, kött, and skärm. Predict the sound, listen, then repeat each word twice.

activity.label: Sound detective
activity.title: Look at the letter after g, k, or sk, then predict the sound
activity.instructions: Front vowel (e, i, y, ä, ö) next? The sound usually softens. Back vowel (a, o, u, å)? It stays hard. Choose, then listen.

items.why: G + ä, a front vowel: it starts like Swedish j.
K + i, a front vowel: the soft tj sound.
A is a back vowel, so sk stays hard: s + k.
Sk + ä, a front vowel: the sj sound.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
A is a back vowel, so k stays hard.
K + ö: Ö is rounded but still a front vowel, so k softens.
Sj is always the sj sound, whatever vowel follows.
U is a back vowel, so sk stays hard.
K + ö, a front vowel: the tj sound.
Skj is always the sj sound, even before o.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
Tj is always the tj sound.
Sk + i: the sj sound, as in Solen skiner.

activity.summary: One question does most of the work: which vowel comes next? Front vowels (e, i, y, ä, ö) soften g, k and sk into three different sounds; back vowels leave them hard. Sj, skj and tj keep their sound whatever follows. Some loanwords break the rule, so trust the recording.

sections.title: Recognise the remaining Lesson 1 spellings
body: Recognition only today: SJ and SKJ normally use the sj sound, as in sjuk and skjorta. Initial HJ and LJ normally begin with the Swedish j sound, as in hjälp and ljus.
Dialect matters in Finland: Sweden-Swedish often merges RS in kurs into a retroflex sound, while Finland-Swedish usually keeps R + S. Many Finland-Swedish speakers also keep a clear D in djur.
Och is /ɔk/ in careful speech and is often shorter in conversation. Skönt normally means pleasant or comfortable; say fint hår or snyggt hår for a natural compliment.

examples.note: Two spellings for the sj sound.
Initial H or L is silent in these spellings; begin with Swedish j.
You may hear j alone in Sweden or a retained d in Finland-Swedish.
Keep r + s separate for a Finland-Swedish target.

examples.fi: Jag gillar din rosa skjorta. Du har fint hår.
examples.en: I like your pink shirt. You have nice hair.
examples.note: The textbook uses skönt hår; fint hår is the natural compliment to produce.

sections.memoryTip: These are recognition words, not a second test. Your target is to notice the spelling and accept dialect variation.
sections.tryIt: Listen once to sjuk, skjorta, hjälp, ljus, djur, kurs, and mars. Copy the Finland-Swedish model you want to use; do not force every word into one accent.

assignment.title: Episode 1 mission: Say who you are
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say your real four-line introduction once slowly and once at normal speed: name, home now, origin, and languages.

ONE SOUND LOOP: Choose only one: tak/tack OR gillar/kött/skärm. Listen and repeat the small set three times.

RETURN: Close the model and give your real introduction from memory in under 20 seconds.
assignment.model:
Hej! Jag heter Alex.
Jag bor i Helsingfors.
Jag kommer från Indien.
Jag talar hindi, engelska och lite svenska.

takeaways: Core: say Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar … as four complete chunks.
Mouth first, audio second: use the Hindi/Marathi/English bridge to find the shape, then copy the Swedish model.
Practise one contrast at a time: tak/tack or the g → j, k → tj, sk → sj pattern.
